newsitem.title: VATICAN: St Peter's in Rome to get facelift for 2000.
newsitem.headline: St Peter's in Rome to get facelift for 2000.

text.p: The Vatican unveiled a plan on Thursday to restore the facade of St Peter's Basilica to its original glory in time for the start of the third millennium.

Parts of the facade, almost as big as a football field, will be covered by scaffolding during the three-year project to clean the marble and repair damage done by four centuries of natural decay, exposure to the elements and pollution.
The work on the largest church in Christendom starts next month and is due to be completed in September 1999.
By then, millions of pilgrims and tourists are expected to begin flocking to Rome for the start of Christianity's third millennium in 2000, which Pope John Paul has declared a special Holy Year.

The nine billion lire ($5.4 million) facelift is being carried out in cooperation with Italy's energy giant ENI, which will provide the Vatican with the technological know-how gained from the geological part of its oil exploration experience.
Technology such as magnetic resonance used in the study of cores drilled from oil fields will determine the condition of the 17th century facade, officials told a news conference.
Ultra-sound devices will be used to assess the physical state of the materials making up the facade.
Graced by eight towering columns, the facade measures 114 metres wide by 45 metres high and is built mostly of tavertine marble that has turned a smudgy brown.
Designed by architect Carlo Maderno and completed in 1614, it includes the central balcony where Popes make their first public appearance after they are elected in secret conclaves.

Popes also use the balcony twice a year at Christmas and Easter for their "Urbi et Orbi" (to the city and the world) blessing and message. Vatican officials said the balcony would be accessible and visible for most of the restoration.

"In four centuries the facade has seen structural fatigue, earthquakes, environmental damage, and ageing of materials. All this will be studied," said professor Pierluigi Silvan, head of the Vatican department in charge of of the church.
He said that acid rain, pollution, nitrogen oxides, and sulphur oxides had been particularly harmful to the marble.
Pollution, pigeons, water seepage and rust have damaged the statues of Christ and the twelve apostles looking down on St Peter's Square from the roof of the facade.
Silvan said, however, that he did not think any of the statues at the top of the facade would have to be replaced by copies despite the damage.
Monitoring equipment installed during the restoration will allow technicians to control atmospheric changes inside the facade or in Michelangelo's dome above it. The data will be sent to a computer.
"This will give us a complete and real-time analysis of the state of health of the basilica at any time," Silvan said.
The first phase of the restoration will start with the left and right sections of the facade. Restorers will then work their way towards the centre for the final stage.
Franco Bernabe, managing director of ENI, did not say how much of the cost would be picked up by the energy giant.
He said the project was not technically sponsorship because the company was always interested in improving its knowledge of the effects of fuel on the urban environment.
